about.headingHtml: I like turning hard technical ideas into working software✦✦
paragraphs: I'm a software engineer with a background in math and computer science. I got into this through problem solving and proofs, and that still shapes the way I work today.

Right now I'm doing my M.S. in Computer Science at Georgia Tech. I've worked on ML pipelines, deep learning projects, and computational geometry research, and I also hold the AWS Certified Developer - Associate certification.
What I enjoy most is going from a rough idea to something real: understanding the problem, building the system, and being able to explain the tradeoffs clearly.

items.title: Undergraduate Research
items.summary: Computational geometry research on faster Order-2 Delaunay triangulation algorithms and higher-order refinement behavior.
bullets: Developed a novel incremental algorithm for Order-2 Delaunay triangulations, achieving a 23.4% speedup over state-of-the-art Rhomboid Tiling implementations.
Engineered a 3D paraboloid projection framework capable of processing 1000+ data points.
Showed that standard mesh refinement techniques generalize to higher-order triangulations.

items.title: Undergraduate Research
items.summary: Metric geometry research on quotient spaces and the failure of Gromov-Hausdorff distance preservation.
bullets: Co-authored research on Metric Geometry, proving Gromov-Hausdorff distances are not preserved under quotient spaces; published on arXiv:2410.14938 and presented at the UF Math Symposium.
Developed formal proofs demonstrating that distance ratios under group actions can be made arbitrarily large or small, refuting standard stability assumptions.
Constructed specific geometric counter-examples using G-invariant subsets.

header.subtitle: Exploring Angle Optimization in Higher-Order Delaunay Triangulations

research.title: Our Research on Order-K Delaunay Triangulations

blocks.text: Delaunay triangulations are fundamental geometric structures used extensively in computational geometry, computer graphics, and mesh generation. Their popularity stems from optimal angular properties: standard Delaunay triangulations maximize the minimum angle among all possible triangulations, helping create well-shaped triangles.

blocks.title: Research Question:
blocks.text: How can refinement optimize angles in Order-2 Delaunay triangulations? While refinement is well-studied for standard (order-1) Delaunay triangulations, its role in higher-order triangulations remains largely unexplored.

While standard Delaunay triangulations (order-1) use single points as vertices, order-k Delaunay triangulations use k-tuples of points. For order-2, each vertex represents the average (barycenter) of two points from the original set. This creates a more complex structure with interesting angle optimization properties.

A key algorithmic contribution of our work is the development of an incremental construction method using the convex hull lifting technique. This approach provides an elegant geometric interpretation of order-k Delaunay triangulations.

blocks.title: Algorithm Overview
blocks.intro: The algorithm leverages the classical duality between Delaunay triangulations and convex hulls in higher dimensions. For order-2 triangulations, we lift points to 3D space and compute barycenters, then project the lower hull back to the plane.

steps.label: Lift Points:
steps.text: Project each point (x, y) to 3D using the paraboloid z = x^2 + y^2

steps.label: Compute Barycenters:
steps.text: For all pairs of lifted points, calculate their average (barycenter)

steps.label: Convex Hull:
steps.text: Compute the 3D convex hull of these barycenter points

steps.label: Lower Hull Projection:
steps.text: Identify facets with downward-facing normals and project them back to 2D

steps.label: Triangulation:
steps.text: The projected lower hull faces form the order-2 Delaunay triangulation

blocks.challengeText: Computing all O(n^2) barycenters becomes computationally expensive for large point sets. Our research explored optimizations using the rhomboid tiling structure to identify only the relevant barycenters that contribute to the lower hull, avoiding unnecessary computation.

items.title: Angle Optimization
items.text: Order-2 Delaunay triangulations extend the local angle property from order-1, lexicographically maximizing the sorted angle vector among all complete level-2 hypertriangulations.

items.title: Refinement Techniques
items.text: We explored Ruppert's algorithm and mesh smoothing for refinement. While both improve angle histograms, order-2 triangulations converge slower than order-1, with blue triangles replicating order-1 structure and red triangles introducing new angles.

items.title: Algorithmic Efficiency
items.text: The rhomboid tiling algorithm significantly outperforms naive barycenter computation. By leveraging the combinatorial structure of hyperplane arrangements, we identify relevant vertices without examining all possible pairs.

blocks.text: Through extensive experimentation with various point distributions (Gaussian, explosion, convex), we found that:

items: Order-2 triangulations show improvement but retain more small angles than order-1
Blue triangles in order-2 replicate order-1 structure, while red triangles introduce new angles
The rhomboid tiling algorithm outperforms our initial incremental approach
Mesh smoothing provides modest improvements but does not eliminate all problematic angles

blocks.text: Our research opens several avenues for future study:

items.title: Improved Incremental Algorithms
items.text: Developing more efficient incremental construction by identifying relevant barycenters without computing all combinations, possibly using predicted structures from the order-1 triangulation.

items.title: Enhanced Refinement
items.text: Investigating refinement strategies specifically designed for order-2 triangulations to better eliminate problematic angles, particularly those introduced by red triangles.

items.title: Complexity Analysis
items.text: Further study of the size and complexity of order-k Delaunay triangulations for k > 2, and whether similar optimization properties hold for higher orders.

blocks.title: Impact:
blocks.text: This research contributes to our understanding of higher-order Delaunay triangulations and their potential applications in mesh generation, where avoiding poorly-shaped triangles is crucial for numerical stability and accuracy in finite element methods and computational simulations.

header.title: Machine Learning Evaluation & Optimization Study
header.subtitle: An ongoing Georgia Tech machine learning project centered on reproducible evaluation, optimizer ablations, and understanding what actually improves model performance.

status.label: Current state
status.text: This page is still in progress. The supervised learning and optimization sections are done, and the unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning sections will be added next.

overview.title: Evaluation first, optimization second
paragraphs: This page combines the two completed parts of the project so far: a supervised-learning benchmark and a follow-up optimization study built around Adult income classification and Wine quality prediction.

The part I like most is that it is not just about getting one good score. A lot of the real work was building a reproducible evaluation pipeline, choosing metrics that fit the datasets, and then testing which optimization changes actually mattered.

reportSections.title: Supervised learning benchmark
reportSections.summary: I built a reproducible benchmarking pipeline across two classification problems with 48,719 total records, using preprocessing, stratified splits, and cross-validation to compare tree-based, kernel-based, and neural models.
highlights: Used stratified 80/20 train-test splits, 3-fold cross-validation, one-hot encoding for Adult, and feature scaling where appropriate
Evaluated Adult with accuracy, F1, and PR-AUC because the target is imbalanced and threshold choice matters
Evaluated Wine with Macro-F1 to reflect multiclass imbalance instead of relying on raw accuracy

resultCards.title: Adult result
resultCards.text: On Adult, the tuned MLP did best by PR-AUC at 0.7808, with linear SVM not far behind at 0.7657. That suggested the one-hot encoded feature space was close to linear, but still complex enough for the MLP to help.

resultCards.title: Wine result
resultCards.text: On Wine, tuned kNN came out on top by Macro-F1 at 0.4654, ahead of CART and RBF SVM. That matched the idea that a smaller, denser feature space would work well with distance-based methods.

resultCards.title: Main takeaway
resultCards.text: The biggest takeaway was that the dataset changed what mattered. Adult leaned toward linear-style models and PR-AUC, while Wine made more sense with distance-based methods and Macro-F1.

reportSections.title: Optimization and regularization study
reportSections.summary: I reused the strongest MLP from the supervised benchmark and ran optimizer and regularization ablations that cut time-to-target by 45% and steps-to-target by 66% while improving multiclass Macro-F1 to 0.3458.
highlights: Compared Randomized Hill Climbing, Simulated Annealing, and Genetic Algorithms by freezing most of the network and optimizing only the final layer
Ran optimizer ablations on the full Adult MLP across SGD, momentum, Nesterov, Adam, AdamW, and Adam without bias correction
Swept weight decay, early stopping, dropout, and noise-based regularization to test which knobs actually change validation behavior

resultCards.title: Randomized optimization
resultCards.text: Randomized Hill Climbing ended up working best out of the randomized methods, which was not what I expected going in.

resultCards.title: Optimizer behavior
resultCards.text: Momentum clearly helped compared to plain SGD, and the Adam-style optimizers converged well once tuned. But none of them actually beat the earlier supervised-learning baseline on F1, which was a useful result on its own.

resultCards.title: Regularization
resultCards.text: Weight decay was the only regularizer that consistently helped. The best fixed setup got the validation loss down to about 0.3125, while dropout and noise-based regularization did not do much.

takeaways.title: What I think was useful here

items.title: The setup mattered as much as the models
items.text: A lot of the value came from getting the evaluation right: avoiding leakage, choosing the right metrics, and running controlled comparisons instead of just chasing one score.

items.title: A better optimizer does not automatically mean a better model
items.text: The optimization section was helpful partly because many changes improved convergence without clearly improving the final model. That distinction matters.

items.title: Different datasets rewarded different choices
items.text: Adult and Wine behaved differently, and the project made that pretty clear. The feature representation and class imbalance affected which models ended up working best.

items.title: Supervised learning
items.text: Completed model benchmarking and metric-driven analysis across Adult and Wine.

items.title: Optimization
